description: The figure displays three pie charts illustrating the distribution of problem-solving outcomes across different difficulty levels—easy, medium, and hard—under the CoT (Chain-of-Thought) setting, categorized by correctness and knowledge availability. Each chart is divided into four segments representing the combinations of knowledge (N for knowledge present, N− for knowledge absent) and correctness (K+ for correct, K− for incorrect), with corresponding percentages shown within each slice. In the "easy" category, the largest segment is N−K+ (45.9%, yellow), followed by N+K+ (40.6%, teal), N−K− (10.1%, orange), and N+K− (3.3%, red). For "medium" problems, N+K+ accounts for 44.6% (teal), N−K+ is 44.3% (yellow), N−K− is 7.2% (orange), and N+K− is 3.9% (red). In the "hard" category, N−K− is the largest at 36.8% (orange), followed by N−K+ at 36.2% (yellow), N+K+ at 20.1% (teal), and N+K− at 7.0% (red). A legend on the right associates the colors with the four categories: teal for N+K+, yellow for N−K+, orange for N−K−, and red for N+K−. The visual data supports the caption's interpretation that easier problems are primarily limited by knowledge deficits, medium problems are dominated by reasoning errors, and hard problems are constrained by a lack of geometric reasoning integration, reflected in the low proportion of correct answers with knowledge (N+K+).
caption_used: Problem distribution based on correctness under the w/ knowledge and w/o knowledge settings using CoT. The results indicate that while easier problems are primarily hindered by a lack of knowledge (N−K+ at approximately 50%), medium problems show a consistent dominance of reasoning-based errors (N−K− at 15%). For hard problems, the primary bottleneck lies in the inability to integrate geometric reasoning, as evidenced by the sharp decline in N+K+ to below 10%.
